title: Longest Common Prefix — vertical scan comparing characters.
shortTitle: Longest Common Prefix — Vertical Scan Comparing Characters

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Common Prefix problem finds the longest starting substring shared by every string in a list. The vertical-scan solution walks character positions left to right, and at each position checks that the character matches across all strings, stopping at the first position where any string ends or disagrees. It runs in time proportional to the total characters examined, which is at most the number of strings times the prefix length.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a set of account numbers that may share a common branch prefix, and a clerk wants the longest leading portion identical across all of them. The clerk reads the first character of every number: if they all match, keep it and move to the second character, and so on. The moment one number runs out or shows a different character, the shared prefix ends right there.
s1_definition.oneliner: Scan character positions top to bottom across all strings and stop at the first mismatch or end.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Common Prefix problem finds the longest starting substring shared by every string in a list. The vertical-scan solution walks character positions left to right, and at each position checks that the character matches across all strings, stopping at the first position where any string ends or disagrees. It runs in time proportional to the total characters examined, which is at most the number of strings times the prefix length.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a set of account numbers that may share a common branch prefix, and a clerk wants the longest leading portion identical across all of them. The clerk reads the first character of every number: if they all match, keep it and move to the second character, and so on. The moment one number runs out or shows a different character, the shared prefix ends right there.

**One line to remember:** Scan character positions top to bottom across all strings and stop at the first mismatch or end.

sections.s2_technical:
The vertical-scan approach treats the strings like rows of a grid and scans down each column. You take the first string as a reference. For each character position in that reference string, you read the character there and then check every other string at the same position. If any other string is shorter than this position, meaning it has ended, or has a different character, the common prefix is everything before this position, so you return the reference string's substring up to here.

If you get through a position with all strings agreeing, you move to the next position. If you reach the end of the reference string without any mismatch, then the whole reference string is the common prefix, because no string disagreed and none was shorter than the reference at any checked position. This handles the case where the shortest string is itself the full prefix.

The reason this is efficient is that it stops as soon as the prefix ends, so in the common case where the shared prefix is short, you examine very few characters even if the strings are long. The worst case, where all strings are identical, examines every character once per string, which is the total input size, and that is unavoidable because you must read the whole prefix to confirm it.

A senior point is the empty and single-element edge cases. If the list is empty, the common prefix is the empty string. If any string is empty, the common prefix is immediately empty because an empty string shares no leading character. A single string's common prefix is itself. Handling these up front avoids index errors in the scan.

Another senior point is alternative strategies and their trade-offs. Horizontal scanning folds the prefix pairwise across strings, binary search on the prefix length tests candidate lengths, and a trie stores all strings and walks the single shared path. Vertical scan is usually the clearest and has the best early-exit behavior when prefixes are short, which is typical for account numbers sharing a branch code. I mention the alternatives to show breadth, then justify the vertical scan for this workload.

A small finance-domain example: `for(int i=0;i<first.length();i++){ char c=first.charAt(i); for(String s:nums){ if(i>=s.length() || s.charAt(i)!=c) return first.substring(0,i); } } return first;` finds the shared branch prefix.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has a batch of account numbers that may begin with a shared branch and product prefix, and a feature extracts the longest leading portion common to all of them to label the batch by its common origin. The batch can be large, so the scan should stop as soon as the shared prefix ends. Finding the longest common prefix by vertical scan is exactly this.

This is exactly how Longest Common Prefix works in Java — scanning each character position across all strings and stopping at the first mismatch or end.

Problem 2 — The batch might be empty or contain an empty account number, in which case the common prefix is empty, and it might contain just one number, whose prefix is itself. This shows the empty-list, empty-string, and single-element edge cases.

What the code will do: a `PrefixExtractor` with `longestCommonPrefix(List<String> numbers)` using a vertical scan with the edge-case guards. The demo extracts the common prefix from a batch of account numbers.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the account-number batch `SAV2001, SAV2002, SAV2015`.

Step 1: the list is non-empty, so we take the first number `SAV2001` as the reference. We scan position zero, character `S`, and check all numbers: all have `S` at position zero, so we keep it and move on.

Step 2: position one is `A`, and all numbers have `A` there, so we keep it. Position two is `V`, all match. Position three is `2`, all match. Position four is `0`, all match. So far the prefix is `SAV20`.

Step 3: position five is `0` in the reference. We check the numbers: `SAV2001` has `0`, `SAV2002` has `0`, but `SAV2015` has `1` at position five, a mismatch. So the common prefix is everything before position five, the substring `SAV20`.

Step 4: we return `SAV20` immediately without scanning any further positions, demonstrating the early exit as soon as the shared prefix ends.

Step 5: for the mixed batch `SAV2001, CUR3001`, position zero is `S` in the reference but `C` in the second number, an immediate mismatch, so the common prefix is the substring before position zero, the empty string, returned at once.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T20:50:00Z INFO Common prefix = 'SAV20'
2026-10-26T20:50:00Z INFO Result = SAV20
2026-10-26T20:50:00Z INFO Common prefix = ''
2026-10-26T20:50:00Z INFO Result =
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: ["SAV2001","SAV2002","SAV2015"]  reference="SAV2001"
    │
    ▼
  for each position i: check char across all strings
    │ i0 'S' all match ; i1 'A' ; i2 'V' ; i3 '2' ; i4 '0' all match
    │ i5 '0' vs "SAV2015"[5]='1' → MISMATCH
    ▼
  return reference.substring(0,5) = "SAV20"
    ▼
  Output: longest common prefix  (mixed batch → "")
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Common Prefix finds the longest starting substring shared by every string in a list, and I solve it with a vertical scan. I treat the strings like rows of a grid and scan down each column: taking the first string as a reference, for each character position I check that every other string has the same character there, and I stop at the first position where any string has ended or shows a different character, returning the reference substring up to that point.

If I get through the whole reference string without any disagreement, the entire reference is the common prefix, which correctly covers the case where the shortest string is itself the full prefix. The efficiency comes from the early exit: when the shared prefix is short, which is typical for account numbers sharing a branch code, I examine very few characters even if the strings are long, and the worst case of identical strings reads the whole input once, which is unavoidable.

I handle the edge cases up front: an empty list or an empty string yields an empty prefix, and a single string's prefix is itself, which keeps the scan from indexing out of bounds. I also know the alternatives, horizontal pairwise folding, binary search on the prefix length, and a trie, and I choose the vertical scan here because it is the clearest and has the best early-exit behavior for short prefixes.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to label a batch of account numbers by the longest leading portion common to all of them, extracting a shared branch and product prefix to identify the batch's origin, stopping as soon as the shared part ended. Explaining the column scan, the early-exit efficiency, the edge-case guards, and awareness of the alternative strategies shows the interviewer that I can pick the right approach for the workload rather than reciting one method.
